notes: The case concerns the sale, lease, and consolidation powers of railway corporations, not compensated residential occupancy.
The case concerns uncompensated railroad appropriation of a landowner's right of way, not residential letting.
The case is a title and cotenancy dispute involving a homestead, with no compensated occupancy at issue.
The police-power discussion concerns railroad freight delivery and interstate commerce, not lodging regulation.

holding_summary: A householder's middle rental parcel remained part of the homestead because he continued using its cistern for family purposes. A separately enclosed residence built and permanently leased for income lost its homestead character because the owner abandoned its domestic use.

quotes.text: This house with its appurtenances had been leased ever since its construction and was occupied by a tenant when this suit was brought.

The language quoted is strictly applicable to the middle lot in controversy. The appellee after moving into his new dwelling and after renting the old continued to use the cistern attached to the middle lot for the purposes of his family.

But from the opinion in the case cited the principle is deducible that when the owner of a parcel of land in a town or city occupied by him as the homestead of his family permanently devotes a part thereof to a purpose inconsistent with its use as a part of his homestead, and permanently abandons such use, the parcel so set apart ceases to be a part of the homestead.
This shows that he never intended wholly to abandon the use of it for domestic purposes.
This evinces a permanent abandonment of the use of the lot under consideration for homestead purposes.

notes: The owner lived on the same original parcel, rented his former dwelling for use as a boarding house, boarded with an early tenant, and continuously leased two residences for income; the decision distinguishes rental property retaining a domestic connection from property permanently separated for income use.
Although an underlying multi-year hotel lease is mentioned, the decision concerns injunction pleading and setoff of unliquidated damages rather than lodging rights or regulation.
The case concerns jurisdiction and partition among cotenants of rural land, not residential occupancy.
The weekly rental was of a bed and bedding rather than rooms or a dwelling; the case concerns forcible repossession of that personal property.
The case concerns riparian water rights, a dam, and a revocable license unrelated to residential occupancy.
Tenants and rents appear only as evidence of possession in a mortgage and title dispute; no dwelling or lodging arrangement is adjudicated.

holding_summary: The partner and his wife occupied the upper story under a joint-occupancy arrangement connected to the parties' business, not as tenants at will. The building owner wrongfully excluded them without warning and remained liable for actual and exemplary damages.

quotes.text: The evidence, however, did not tend to show that appellee was a tenant at will or even strictly a tenant at all, but did tend to show a joint-occupancy of the house for the conduct of a business in which they were-both interested
Appellee is shown to have been entitled to the occupancy of the house at the time its doors were closed upon him.
This was done without warning, and so far as appears from the evidence without necessity.
Appellant's action was arbitrary and looked toward oppression.

notes: The occupancy lasted from approximately February through August 1882 and arose from the parties' partnership rather than a separately stated rent.
The alleged tenancy at will concerned unspecified city lots, and the court found that no landlord-tenant contract existed.
The case concerns liability for forcibly taking and damaging a farm occupant's personal property, without adjudicating a compensated occupancy arrangement.
Leasing farmland to tenants appears only in an adverse-possession dispute and does not involve dwellings, rooms, or lodging regulation.

holding_summary: A person who controlled adjoining premises and knowingly leased them for prostitution was liable for the resulting nuisance and injury to the neighboring residence, whether he owned the premises or acted as an agent.

quotes.text: And if Lee controlled the property and leased it to the prostitutes knowingly, as was found by the jury, his liability would follow.
And if Lee controlled the property and leased it to the prostitutes knowingly, as was found by the jury, his liability would follow.

This is an appeal from a judgment allowing damages against the appellant for wilfully, and with intent to injure, leasing premises adjoining the home of the plaintiff, to prostitutes for the purposes of prostitution; it being alleged that the leased premises had been so used after the lease to the annoyance and injury to plaintiffs’, etc.

notes: The decision treats a knowingly harmful commercial use of leased premises adjoining a home as actionable; the duration and operator's precise status are not stated.
The verbal lease at will was expressly without rent and arose only as part of a land-title and constructive-tenancy dispute.
The case concerns a street-railway easement as an incident of land ownership, not residential letting.
The tenant's possession matters only to limitation and title procedure; the case does not concern compensated dwelling or room occupancy.
